name: Cade Cunningham
notes: Oklahoma State's Big 12 Player of the Year (20.1/6.2/3.5, first OSU player so honored since Bob Kurland in the 1940s), a rare big, pass-first lead guard with real feel from a football-QB background. Detroit took him 1st. Cunningham delivered a strong rookie year before a stress fracture wiped out most of 2022-23; he returned to a 22.7 ppg bounce-back, then a full superstar breakout — a 26.1/9.1 All-Star season, All-NBA Third Team, and a 2025-26 All-Star starter/All-NBA First Team campaign (5th in MVP voting) leading Detroit to 60 wins, capped by a 45-point playoff game. Hit: a true franchise-cornerstone No. 1 pick who delivered exactly the star outcome projected, injury notwithstanding.

name: Jalen Green
notes: The first-ever G League Ignite signee, an explosive, Zach-LaVine/Kobe-comped scoring guard with an elite first step and real shooting shortfalls typical of a non-college prospect. Houston took him 2nd. Green developed into a genuine high-volume scorer (four 40-point games before turning 21, a full 82-game 21.0 ppg efficient season in 2024-25) before a 2025 blockbuster trade to Phoenix (part of the Kevin Durant deal) saw him post 17.8 ppg in a swept play-in appearance. Mixed outcome: a real, high-scoring NBA talent whose team success has lagged his individual production.

name: Evan Mobley
notes: USC's rare triple-crown freshman (Pac-12 Player, Defensive Player and Freshman of the Year, matching Anthony Davis) — a "7-foot unicorn" with elite rim protection and passing, real shooting range (30% from three) the flagged concern. Cleveland took him 3rd. Mobley was runner-up Rookie of the Year by the smallest margin in 19 years, developed into an All-Defensive First Teamer, then won the 2025 Defensive Player of the Year (Cleveland's first ever) and made his first All-Star and All-NBA teams, continuing to add offense (18.2 ppg, improved 29.7% from three) in 2025-26. Hit: the exact two-way unicorn upside scouted became a genuine DPOY-level star.

name: Scottie Barnes
notes: A Florida State bench point-forward (10.3/4.1, ACC Rookie of the Year) valued for elite size-athleticism-defensive-versatility, with an already-flagged slow, elbow-drift shooting motion as the clear long-term swing skill. Toronto took him 4th. Barnes won Rookie of the Year immediately, developed into a first-time All-Star by 2023-24 (19.9/8.2/6.1) despite the shooting concerns never fully resolving, signed a $225M extension, and made his second All-Star team and All-Defensive Second Team in 2025-26 (18.1 ppg on an efficient 51%) while dragging Toronto to a Game 7 loss on 24.1 ppg. Hit: a defense-and-versatility bet at 4th overall that became a genuine franchise-player outcome.

name: Jalen Suggs
notes: Gonzaga's clutch five-star freshman (14.4/4.5, a 40-foot Final Four buzzer-beater, consensus Second-Team All-American), elite competitiveness and two-way guard skill from a title-game-losing team. Orlando took him 5th. A fractured thumb and ankle surgery slowed his early development, but Suggs became a genuine two-way piece (All-Defensive Second Team, Orlando's first such honor since Dwight Howard) and signed a $150.5M extension in 2024 — though back spasms and a 2025 arthroscopic knee surgery have made durability a persistent theme. Mixed outcome: real two-way stardom whenever healthy, injuries a recurring interruption.

name: Josh Giddey
notes: An Australian NBL prospect (Adelaide 36ers) who led the league in assists (7.6) and became the first Australian to record consecutive triple-doubles, elite playmaking with real shooting-efficiency concerns already flagged. Oklahoma City took him 6th. Giddey became the youngest player ever with an NBA triple-double, developed into a genuine stat-stuffer (13.8/6.8/7.4 over three OKC seasons) before a 2024 trade to Chicago fully unlocked him — a 2025-26 season averaging 17.0/9.1/8.3 with 10+ triple-doubles and a $100M extension. Solid outcome: real, statistically extraordinary production that has yet to translate into deep team playoff success.

name: Jonathan Kuminga
notes: A five-star recruit who reclassified and joined G League Ignite (15.8/7.2/2.7), athletic upside with real developmental rawness. Golden State took him 7th. Kuminga won a championship at 19 (the second-youngest champion ever), developed real scoring flashes (a 16.1 ppg season, back-to-back 34-point games), before a restricted free agency standoff and a $48.5M extension preceded a February 2026 trade to Atlanta (a strong 27-point debut) and a further September 2026 move to Minnesota. Mixed outcome: real athletic scoring talent and a championship ring, without ever settling into one long-term role.

name: Franz Wagner
notes: A four-star Michigan sophomore (13.0 ppg, team-leading in steals and blocks, Second/Third-Team All-Big Ten), real two-way versatility and feel. Orlando took him 8th. Wagner delivered immediately — All-Rookie First Team — and grew every season (15.2 to 18.6 to 19.7 to a 24.2 ppg 2024-25 breakout), signing a $224M extension in 2024 and remaining Orlando's franchise centerpiece into 2026. Hit: steady, uninterrupted growth from rookie to legitimate All-NBA-caliber star.

name: Davion Mitchell
notes: Baylor's Naismith and NABC Defensive Player of the Year as a junior, an elite point-of-attack defender who helped win the 2021 national title (15/6/5 in the championship game), with offensive consistency and shooting the flagged concern. Sacramento took him 9th. Mitchell's rookie year (11.5/4.2) suggested real promise, but his role shrank sharply the next two seasons before a 2024 trade to Toronto and a 2025 move to Miami finally found him a real fit (10.3/5.3 across 30 games), re-signing for $24M. Bust relative to a lottery slot, though a genuine, revived defensive-guard role by 2025.

name: Ziaire Williams
notes: Stanford's top-ranked small forward recruit nationally and the program's first five-star since 2014, a triple-double flash (12/12/10) on an otherwise modest, still-developing freshman season (10.7/4.6 on 37.4% FG). New Orleans took him 10th (traded to Memphis). Williams's promising rookie year (8.1 ppg) was interrupted by a 2022-23 knee injury and a scoring dip, before a 2024 trade to Brooklyn found him a real role (10.0 ppg), a $12.5M extension, and a 2026 move to the Lakers. Bust relative to a top-10, former-No.-1-recruit billing, though a real NBA rotation player has emerged.

name: James Bouknight
notes: UConn's First-Team All-Big East sophomore (18.7/5.7, a 40-point game against Creighton), real scoring punch clouded by a torn high-school meniscus and a sophomore-year elbow surgery that limited him to 15 games. Charlotte took him 11th. Bouknight never developed (79 games across three seasons, 4.8 ppg on 36.3% FG), waived in 2024 and cut loose by Portland the next day, his career shifting to Mexico's G League circuit. Bust: real scoring talent that the flagged durability concerns compounded into a lost NBA opportunity.

name: Joshua Primo
notes: A five-star Alabama freshman and the youngest player in college basketball (8.1/3.4, SEC All-Freshman), real long-term upside on a thin, young sample. San Antonio took him 12th, making him the youngest college-attending player ever to appear in an NBA game. Primo's on-court chance ended abruptly — released by the Spurs in October 2022 citing mental health concerns, followed by allegations that he exposed himself to a team psychologist (charges were investigated and declined for insufficient evidence in December 2023). A brief 2023-24 Clippers look didn't stick, and he's since played in Russia's VTB League. Bust: real developmental talent, career derailed by circumstances far beyond basketball performance.

name: Chris Duarte
notes: Oregon's Jerry West Award winner as the nation's top shooting guard and AP Third-Team All-American (17.1 ppg on 53.2/42.4% shooting), a mature, two-way senior with elite efficiency. Indiana took him 13th. Duarte set a franchise rookie-debut scoring record (27 points) and made All-Rookie Second Team, but production collapsed every season after (13.1 to 7.9 to 3.9 to 2.1 ppg) across Indiana, Sacramento and Chicago. Bust: a polished, efficient college star whose NBA production fell off a cliff almost immediately after a strong debut.

name: Moses Moody
notes: Arkansas's SEC Freshman of the Year (16.8/5.8, First-Team All-SEC), real shooting and size for a wing with shot-selection efficiency (42.7% FG) the flag. Golden State took him 14th. Moody won a championship as a rookie in a bench role, then developed patiently (4.4 to 8.1 to 9.8 ppg) into a real contributor, signing a $39M extension in 2024 and breaking out fully in 2025-26 (12.1/3.3/1.6 across 60 games) before a torn patellar tendon ended his season in March 2026. Mixed outcome: a genuine, steadily-improving NBA wing and champion, injury interrupting a real breakout year.

name: Corey Kispert
notes: Gonzaga's Julius Erving Award winner and consensus First-Team All-American (18.6/5.0 on 52.9/44% shooting, a 32-point/9-three game against Virginia), elite shooting with limited ball-handling as the natural specialist trade-off. Washington took him 15th. Kispert developed steadily (8.2 to 11.1 to 13.4 ppg), signed a $54M extension in 2024, battled a torn thumb ligament in 2025, and was traded to Atlanta in January 2026 (part of the Trae Young deal) — posting a career-high 33 points against his former team soon after. Mixed outcome: a real, valuable NBA shooting specialist for years, never quite a full go-to scorer.

name: Alperen Şengün
notes: A skilled, advanced-feel Turkish big man (comps ranging from Sabonis and Vučević to Kevin Love) whose defense was the clear scouting concern, dropping a lottery-caliber talent to 16th. Oklahoma City took him (traded to Houston). Şengün became a starter after Christian Wood's trade, developed into a genuine two-way force — a $185M extension, back-to-back All-Star selections (the second-ever Turkish All-Star), and a 2025-26 season averaging 20.4/6.2 assists as Houston's franchise cornerstone. Hit: a lottery-grade talent whose defensive question never stopped him from becoming a genuine All-Star center.

name: Trey Murphy III
notes: A Rice-to-Virginia transfer who completed a rare 50-40-90 shooting season as a junior, elite efficiency on modest volume (11.3/3.4) that had scouts split on his exact ceiling. Memphis took him 17th (traded to New Orleans). Murphy developed into a genuine scoring wing — a $112M extension, a 21.2 ppg 2024-25 peak before a season-ending shoulder injury — and returned in 2025-26 to break the franchise three-point record and post a career-high 44-point game. Hit: elite shooting efficiency that scaled into real high-volume NBA scoring.

name: Tre Mann
notes: A five-star Florida sophomore breakout (16.0/5.6/3.5, First-Team All-SEC) after a modest freshman year, real point-guard upside on a still-developing sample. Oklahoma City took him 18th. Mann developed gradually (a 24-12-12 triple-double in 2023) before a 2024 trade to Charlotte (a $24M re-signing) and further move to Washington by 2026. Bust relative to a lottery-adjacent slot, though a real, sustained NBA guard role across three teams.

name: Kai Jones
notes: Texas's Big 12 Sixth Man of the Year (8.8/4.8), praised for elite work ethic by coach Shaka Smart, real athletic upside on modest sophomore production. New York took him 19th (traded to Charlotte). Jones barely played (2.7 ppg over two seasons) before a 2023 release following erratic, incoherent social media posts; a G League and Clippers detour led to a real Dallas flash (11.4 ppg on strong efficiency) in 2024-25 before a move to Turkish basketball. Bust: real athletic tools that off-court struggles and thin opportunity never let develop into consistent NBA production.

name: Jalen Johnson
notes: A consensus five-star Duke recruit (19/19 in his debut) who left college mid-season in February 2021 after 13 games (11.2/6.2/2.0), real top-shelf talent evaluated on an unusually thin, injury-and-departure-shortened sample. Atlanta took him 20th. Johnson needed three patient developmental seasons before a real breakout (16.0/8.7 in 2023-24, a $150M extension) and a superstar-level 2025-26 (22.5/7.9 ast, 13 triple-doubles, first All-Star selection and All-NBA Third Team) after recovering from 2025 shoulder surgery. Hit: a top-of-the-class talent whose thin college sample undersold a genuine late-blooming star.
